newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices hit 2-1/2 week lows, soybeans drop.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices hit 2-1/2 week lows, soybeans drop.

text.p: Coffee prices fell sharply on Monday as worries about tight supplies eased with reports of rising stocks at coffee warehouses.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, May coffee ended down 17.70 cents a pound at 168.65 cents, the biggest one-day drop in prices since the current rally began in early December and the lowest close since February 25.
"I think the party is over," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "Things are not as bullish as they were two weeks ago."

May futures had hit a high of 209.50 cents on March 5, rising from a low of 101.15 cents on December 6. Frantic buying from speculators and coffee roasters had been sparked by strikes in key producer Colombia and prospects for lower production there and in Mexico and Brazil this year.

Those factors had caught many coffee roasters short of supply at a time newly harvested Central American coffee is usually moving north. But that movement appears to have picked up in recent weeks, as stocks data demonstrated on Monday.

The exchange reported that warehouse coffee stocks certified for delivery against futures rose for a seventh straight day on Friday, up 2,250 bags to 47,233 bags -- about triple the level of two weeks ago.

After the close of trading, the Green Coffee Association of New York in its monthly stocks report also eased supply concerns. The GCA said supplies of green coffee stowed in U.S. warehouses rose by 204,000 bags in February to 1,546,000 bags -- their highest level in five months. Most dealers expected the February data to show a rise of up to 100,000 bags.
Each bag of coffee weighs 132 pounds.

Professional commodity fund investors also bailed out of the soybean market, which last week had soared to 8-1/2 year highs. At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed down 24-1/2 cents a bushel at $8.25.

Soybeans last week seesawed wildly as traders worried that U.S. prices, driven by record demand from processors, were so high that even newly harvested Brazilian soybeans might be imported. Prices on Monday gave back almost all Friday's gain.
"Today the trade gained a little bit of confidence that we've reached a level where demand is going to slow down with competition from South America," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.
Traders also pointed to an announcement by Cargill Inc that three of its large processing plants would shut down temporarily this summer due to reduced profit margins.
Corn prices shrugged off the weakness in the nearby soybean pit, with May corn closing up 2-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.06-3/4 on indications of strong livestock feed demand.

A report on Friday by the Agriculture Department estimated that 1.527 million cattle were placed on feed in February in the seven leading cattle feeding states, six percent more than in the same month a year earlier. Analysts had expected the placements to rise only 4.3 percent.
"It was supported a little from the cattle on feed report," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed lower but traders said the market was building a foundation for a possible price rally led by gasoline as spring and the summer travel season approaches.
April crude closed down 37 cents at $20.92 a barrel.
"We could easily test $20.00, but we are setting the stage for a comeback that takes us to $23.00 in a seasonal rally," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co.
Crude led refined products lower with April gasoline ending at 65.26 cents a gallon, down 0.51 cent, and April heating oil at 54.30 cents a gallon, down 1.03 cents.
"We were just shaking out some weak longs in a typical consolidation," said Mike DeLuca, a dealer with Prudential Securities.
